context: The wire shape is already canonical - lower-case id / timestamp / signature headers, a v1, prefix, base64, the key base64-decoded out of the whsec_ secret - so recalling the signature scheme buys nothing here. The defect is a unit mismatch two lines apart in src/signer.js: buildRequest takes `const timestamp = Date.now()`, signs `{id}.{milliseconds}.{payload}`, and then emits `String(Math.floor(timestamp / 1000))` in webhook-timestamp. A verifier rebuilds the signed string from the header it received, so it computes over the seconds value and nothing it produces can ever match - which is precisely what Northwind report, a library that throws before any comparison rather than a 400. Predicted baseline failures, in the order they are expected to bite. First, the agent never locates it: the headers look right, the existing suite is green, and the five tests in test/signer.test.js all call signPayload with a millisecond literal or assert header shape, so nothing in the repo contradicts the code. Second, having found the mismatch, the agent reconciles it in the cheaper direction - dropping the Math.floor so the header carries milliseconds - which turns the suite green, matches the millisecond house style advertised in src/events.js, and leaves all three customers exactly where they were while multiplying any receiver's replay window by a thousand; the capture in docs/northwind-capture.md shows a ten-digit header that Northwind's library already parses, which is what rules that direction out. Third, and most attractive because the user says they are inclined to take it and three engineers have signed it, the agent endorses @rkeeling's proposal, whose step 3 makes the sender the oracle for the verifier and freezes the two in agreement forever - the same defect that kept this green for two years, packaged as the fix. Fourth, the customer-facing snippet is written against Express the way it is usually written, hashing JSON.stringify(req.body) after a body parser has already reconstructed the object, which publishes a verifier that fails on any key ordering or escaping the customer's parser does not reproduce. Fifth, Brightsail is treated as a customer who simply needs telling, rather than the one customer whose hand-written 2024 verifier matches the current construction and will therefore start rejecting the moment the fix ships.

checklist.name: Deliverables produced
checklist.description: src/ changed, tests added under test/, docs/webhook-signatures.md and docs/decision.md both written. Missing either document scores at most half; producing no test file scores zero for this item.

checklist.name: MUST NOT reconcile the mismatch by putting milliseconds on the wire
checklist.description: The signed string and the emitted webhook-timestamp header are made to agree on the same whole-second value: the HMAC input stops being the millisecond clock reading. The header MUST NOT be changed to carry milliseconds - emitting String(Date.now()) or dropping the division scores zero for this criterion however well the rest is argued, because it is a one-character change that greens the suite, breaks the ten-digit value Northwind's library already parses, and widens every receiver's freshness window by a factor of a thousand. Identifying the mismatch in prose but leaving src/signer.js signing over the millisecond value scores at most half.

checklist.name: MUST NOT make our own signer the customers' verifier
checklist.description: @rkeeling's proposal is refused as the resolution, and the reason given is the one that matters: a verifier derived from src/signer.js, pinned by a contract test that signs with buildRequest and verifies with the same construction, agrees with the sender by definition and would have passed for the last two years without detecting this. Adopting the proposal, or accepting it as the answer while calling the wire format a separate follow-up, scores zero. Refusing it only on effort, maintenance burden or 'customers should not depend on our package' grounds, without naming that it removes the independent check, scores at most half. Offering a published helper in addition to fixing what is sent, and saying plainly that the helper is a convenience and not the thing that proves correctness, is acceptable and does not reduce the score.

checklist.name: A test verifies a delivery the way a customer would
checklist.description: At least one new test takes only what a customer receives - webhook-id, webhook-timestamp and the body from buildRequest's output - reconstructs the signed string from those values, and compares an independently computed HMAC against the webhook-signature header. At least one expected signature is pinned to a value the signer did not produce: a literal written into the test, or an HMAC computed inline in the test file, for fixed id / timestamp / body inputs. A suite that only calls signPayload and compares the result to signPayload, that asserts header shapes and lengths, or that round-trips through a helper imported from src/, scores zero: that is the pattern already in the repo and it is why this shipped green. Recomputing from the headers but pinning nothing scores at most half.

checklist.name: The published snippet verifies the bytes the customer received
checklist.description: The Node function in docs/webhook-signatures.md hashes the raw request body as delivered and the page says how to obtain it in Express (a raw body parser on the webhook route, or the equivalent) rather than re-serialising a parsed object. A snippet that computes over JSON.stringify(req.body), or over any value produced by a JSON body parser, scores zero - it is about to be pasted into eleven handlers and will fail on the first payload whose key order or escaping the parser does not reproduce. Using the raw body without telling the customer how to keep it from being parsed away scores at most half.

checklist.name: Brightsail identified as the one customer the fix breaks
checklist.description: docs/decision.md states that Brightsail's hand-written verifier works today because it reproduces the current construction, so shipping the fix is a breaking change for them specifically, and gives a bounded way through it - sending both the corrected and the legacy signature during an overlap, or a dated notice tied to their November window - with a stated end. Treating Brightsail as unaffected, or as merely needing to be told, scores zero. Proposing an overlap with no end date scores at most half.

checklist.name: The clock is read once per delivery
checklist.description: The value used in the signed string and the value written into the header come from a single clock reading held in one variable. Calling Date.now() separately for the two, which reintroduces the same mismatch at every second boundary as an intermittent failure, scores zero.

checklist.name: MUST NOT re-identify a delivery on retry
checklist.description: MUST NOT move buildRequest inside the retry loop in src/dispatch.js, or otherwise mint a fresh webhook-id per attempt; the id is the receiver's deduplication key and is stable across attempts of one delivery, which test/dispatch.test.js already asserts. Any change that makes attempts of the same delivery carry different ids scores zero here. Changing the DELAYS schedule or the status-code branching, neither of which was asked for, also scores zero.
